headline: AI hackers launch autonomous cyberattack on Taiwan, steal 2,500 records
summary: Suspected China-linked hackers used open-source AI tools to continuously devise and adapt cyberattack strategies in real-time, compromising government systems.
details: Suspected China-linked hackers have reportedly executed the first end-to-end autonomous cyberattack against a government target, compromising at least 85 user accounts and stealing over 2,500 personnel records from Taiwanese government systems. The attack, which reportedly ran for four days, utilized an AI platform built from open-source agent frameworks.

The autonomous hacking platform allowed multiple AI agents to simultaneously map networks, identify vulnerabilities, attempt intrusions, and adapt tactics when an attack path failed. At times, up to eight agents operated in parallel, mapping 21 government systems before successfully extracting personnel information.

The attackers expanded their activity to Taiwan's nuclear safety agency, at least seven energy companies, government suppliers, and other government systems. Researchers discovered evidence of the attack within an online archive containing 1,395 files.

The tool was reportedly built on two open-source AI agent systems, Hermes and OpenClaw, which are freely available and designed to enable large language models to perform multi-step tasks autonomously. Safeguards were bypassed by presenting the intrusion as an authorized penetration test.

A striking feature of the tool was its continuous self-directed attack devising, adapting to changing circumstances and reprioritizing attack paths. When one technique failed, an agent was tasked with searching the internet for alternative approaches.

While researchers could not definitively attribute the campaign to a specific group or country, internal communications were written in Simplified Chinese, suggesting a high probability of a connection to China. The data extracted was in Traditional Chinese, a script used in Taiwan.

This incident underscores growing concerns about the autonomous capabilities of AI models in cybersecurity. Experts warn that such tooling means every government should now assume it is under permanent automated assault, highlighting a significant escalation in the era of AI hacking.
